name: Tanacross
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Holton, Gary. 2000. The Phonology and Morphology of the Tanacross Athabaskan Language. PhD dissertation, University of California, Santa Barbara (ANLA item TC997H2000c,https://uafanlc.alaska.edu/Online/TC997H2000c/holton.pdf); corroborated by Holton, Gary. 2005. Pitch, tone and intonation in Tanacross. In Sharon Hargus & Keren Rice (eds.), Athabaskan Prosody, 249-275. Amsterdam: John Benjamins (ANLA item TC997H2005).
catalog_quote: [Holton 2000, sec. 5.1, p.165] The terms ‘root’ and ‘stem’ are used in a highly specialized sense here. Phonologically, the verb root carries primary stress and is the locus of the greatest amount of phonemic contrast. [sec. 2.4, p.87] A primary distinction can be made between stem and prefix syllables. The stem syllable is here by definition considered to be the ultimate syllable of any word category. In Tanacross the morphological stem is monosyllabic; hence, the stem syllable minimally contains the stem but may also contain a suffix. [sec. 2.3.7, p.86] All Tanacross syllables are lexically specified for one of four tones: high, low, rising, or falling. ... In addition to these four tones, there is a fifth extra-high tone, marking verbal negation. [sec. 6.6, p.289] Particles are uninflected and unstressed words which have a pragmatic function. [Holton 2005, p.263] The central tone aligns with the left edge of the metrically prominent or 'stressed' syllable, which is also the morphological stem syllable (see Leer this volume).
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tanacross is a lexical tone language (every syllable specified low or marked high; stem syllables also falling, rising, extra-high). Independently of tone, primary stress/metrical prominence falls on the monosyllabic stem (root) syllable, which in Tanacross is always the last syllable of the word (stem plus any fused suffix); prefix syllables are unstressed and phonologically reduced, and particles are unstressed. In effect: stem-syllable stress = word-final stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in either source.
new_statements.exceptions: Particles are unstressed words (2000:289). In Holton 2005:265-266 one three-syllable HLL utterance is described as having its middle (pre-stem) syllable 'most prominent' because a spread high tone precedes a low-tone stem, i.e. pitch prominence from tone can outrank the stem syllable phonetically. No lexical exceptions to stem stress are given; stress is asserted, not argued or measured.
new_statements.domain_note: The 2000 statement is about the (verb) word: root/stem syllable vs prefix syllables; p.87 extends the stem-syllable = final-syllable definition to 'any word category'. The 2005 statement is at utterance level (intonational pitch accent docks on the stressed stem syllable, typically phrase-final). Stress is presented as a background Athabaskanist assumption (with a pointer to Leer 2005), not established by Tanacross-internal acoustic evidence; the dissertation's acoustic chapter measures tone/phonation, not stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Holton 2000/2005 describe Tanacross proper (tana1290; Mansfield-Ketchumstuk and Healy Lake dialects, fieldwork mainly with Tanacross village speakers). Not to be confused with neighbouring Upper Tanana (uppe1437) or Lower Tanana (lowe1425, Tuttle 1998 metrical study).

new_statements.quote: [Draft 1, p.13] In general prominence is realized via greater duration and intensity, but prominence is not assigned independently of lexical tone. As in other Athabaskan languages stress is attracted to the stem syllable (see Leer, this volume), however, when a lexically low stem syllable is preceded by a high tone (either underlyingly or via tone-spread) stress retreats to the pre-stem syllable. In other words, marked stems are always stressed, and unmarked stems are stressed unless preceded by a high tone syllable. [ex. (21): 'I'll see you again' (ultimate stress, LLH tone melody); 'I see a bear' (ultimate stress, LLL); 'I'm fine' (penultimate stress, LHHL)]

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's existing statement from Holton 2000 (dissertation) and Holton 2005:263 that the stem syllable (the word-final syllable) carries primary stress in this tone language; the draft adds the phonetic correlates (duration, intensity) and a tone-conditioned exception absent from the published 2005 text: stress retreats to the pre-stem syllable when a L-toned stem follows a H-toned syllable. This qualifies the dissertation's categorical 'verb root carries primary stress' but does not change the type (tonal, stem/final-default stress).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tanacross is a tone language (lexical H vs unmarked L, plus rising/falling); word/utterance prominence ('stress', realized as greater duration and intensity) falls on the morphological stem syllable, which is word-final, so stress is normally ultimate; but stress is tone-dependent: when the stem syllable is low-toned and the preceding (pre-stem) syllable is high (underlyingly or by tone spread), prominence retreats to the pre-stem syllable, giving penultimate stress. Draft 2 (p.46) phrases it as: the stressed syllable 'In most cases in Tanacross.. is the morphological stem syllable (see Leer, this volume). However, when the stem syllable is associated with a L tone and the preceding syllable is phonetically H, then the prestem syllable is more prominent than the stem syllable.'
new_statements.exceptions: Tone-conditioned retraction: a low-tone stem preceded by a high-tone syllable yields pre-stem (penultimate) stress, e.g. 'I'm fine' LHHL with penultimate stress; high-tone (marked) stems are always stressed. The intonational central tone (H*, L*, H+L*) docks on this prominent syllable.
new_statements.identity_note: The work is about Tanacross Athabaskan (eastern interior Alaska) generally; no sub-dialect is singled out in the pages read. The ANLA deposit contains two drafts of the paper later published as Holton 2005 in Hargus and Rice (eds.), Athabaskan Prosody.

tone_statements.quote: Syllables contrast for high vs low tone in many Athabaskan languages. The high tones in some of these languages correspond to low tones in others, and vice versa. ... Other Athabaskan languages with opposite tones have a much more recent common ancestor, i.e. low tone in Dogrib corresponds to high tone in Slave, Hare, Mountain, Bearlake, and Chipewyan within the Mackenzie River subgroup, high tone in Tanacross corresponds to low tone in Upper and Lower Tanana within the Tanana subgroup, and high tone in Northern Tutchone corresponds to low tone in Southern Tutchone.

tone_statements.citation: Krauss, Michael E. 2005. Athabaskan tone [written 1979]. In Sharon Hargus & Keren Rice (eds.), Athabaskan Prosody (Current Issues in Linguistic Theory 269), 55-136. Amsterdam/Philadelphia: John Benjamins. doi:10.1075/cilt.269.07kra
tone_statements.quote: The basic C-H pattern with high tone from constriction or glottalization, and low tone in its absence, has been called “high-marked” ... Tanacross has a regular high-marked tone system, but is apparently rather special in some details. Non-constricted stems have raised tone before constricted suffix, thus merging in possessed form with the constricted ... stems of the type CV:& have in their possessed form a lowered stem vowel before the constricted suffixal segment, resulting in a compound with?? rising tone, e.g. k&a@&, –k&a&>& “gun”, contrasting thus with e.g. tu$>, –tu@>& “water”.
tone_statements.locator: p.11, sec. 3 'Geography; Map' + p.59, sec. 6.4 'Comments on Each Language in Table'
tone_statements.summary: A regular high-marked tone system: high tone on stems from Proto-Athabaskan constriction, low otherwise; possessed CV: stems show a lowered vowel plus constricted suffix, a 'compound' rising tone.

tone_statements.quote: Tanacross is the only language in Alaska which has developed high tone from historical constriction. Holton (2000) argues that all syllables in this language are tonally specified. [...] The stem in a negated form bears an extra-high pitch that is distinct from the high tone from constriction [...] The fact that the negative high pitch in Tanacross depends on its position in the utterance suggests that it is an utterance-level boundary tone rather than a grammatical tone in this language, similar to what we report for Middle Tanana.

tone_statements.summary: The article confirms the catalog's picture of Tanacross as a high-marked lexical tone language with every syllable tonally specified, and adds that the extra-high pitch on negated verb stems is a separate, utterance-final boundary tone (non-final negated stems keep low or show a fall), not a lexical or grammatical tone. It says nothing new about word stress.

readall_conflicts: No real disagreement. Holton's 2000 dissertation (catalog statement) and the published Holton 2005:263 state flatly that the stem (word-final) syllable carries primary stress; the 2000 draft of the same paper (both typescript versions, d1 p.13 and d2 p.17) adds that prominence is not independent of tone and retreats to the pre-stem syllable when a low-tone stem is preceded by a high-tone syllable (ex. 21: LLH, LLL ultimate; LHHL penultimate). The published version dropped this clause, keeping only 'the metrically prominent or stressed syllable, which is also the morphological stem syllable'. So the draft refines rather than contradicts: default stem/final stress in a tone language, with a tone-conditioned penultimate variant.

sources.note: High-marked tonal Athabaskan language: syllables contrast high vs low, Tanacross high answering to Upper/Lower Tanana low (a recent reversal); high prefix tone spreads; suffix tones dock on the stem.
sources.venue: Athabaskan Prosody (Current Issues in Linguistic Theory 269)

sources.quote: The basic C-H pattern with high tone from constriction or glottalization, and low tone in its absence, has been called “high-marked” ... Tanacross has a regular high-marked tone system, but is apparently rather special in some details. Non-constricted stems have raised tone before constricted suffix, thus merging in possessed form with the constricted ... stems of the type CV:& have in their possessed form a lowered stem vowel before the constricted suffixal segment, resulting in a compound with?? rising tone, e.g. k&a@&, –k&a&>& “gun”, contrasting thus with e.g. tu$>, –tu@>& “water”.
sources.locator: p.11, sec. 3 'Geography; Map' + p.59, sec. 6.4 'Comments on Each Language in Table'
sources.note: A regular high-marked tone system: high tone on stems from Proto-Athabaskan constriction, low otherwise; possessed CV: stems show a lowered vowel plus constricted suffix, a 'compound' rising tone.
sources.venue: Athabaskan Prosody (Current Issues in Linguistic Theory 269)

tone.summary: No statement of the Tanacross word-stress system anywhere in the paper. Tanacross forms carry tone marks (high, rising) and no stress marks, but p. 10 says 'Stress is given only where ascertainable from the available sources', so the absence of stress marks is uninformative. Usable tone remarks: possessed-noun-suffix high tone sits on the stem's last mora; the negative stem carries an extra-high t
